utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Case Number IT-99-36-T, The Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, summary of this witness, Mr. Cunningham, was this witness familiar with Radoslav Brdjanin or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: He is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So, Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Ms. Korner, appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Julian Nicholls with Joanna Korner and Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you all. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. I'm with David Cunningham, Aleksandar Vujic, and Kelli Serratt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. We have a new witness. There are no protective measures that I know of or that I have been made aware of. Good morning to you, sir, and welcome to this Tribunal and to The Hague on a nice warm day. You are about to start giving evidence. And before you do so, our Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, a solemn declaration stating that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is on the sheet of paper that you have just been given. Please read that aloud, and that would be your solemn undertaking with us. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Golic, you are going to be first asked a series of questions by Mr. Ackerman, who is the lead counsel for Mr. Brdjanin, who is the accused in this case, as you know. He will then be followed by Mr. Nicholls, I take it, who is appearing for the Prosecution in this case, a member of the team of the Prosecution. You are a Defence witness, but that does not mean that you are here to testify in favour of the accused and against the Prosecution. You are here to tell us the truth. So in other words, you do not have a right to distinguish between the Prosecution and the Defence. Your obligation is to answer all questions truthfully and fully irrespective of where they come. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Ackerman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir, your name is Naum Golic?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber where you live.

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: In Banja Luka, Koste Jacica Street, number 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: The 30th of June 1971.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To whom are you married?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Suzana.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your wife a Serb?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is her ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: She is not. She is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have children?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you working these days? And if so, what are you doing?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I work for an insurance company, and I own a small shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you -- I'm going back now to the 1990s or earlier even maybe. Did you ever serve in the army?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell the Chamber when and where you served in the army.

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: I served in 1989 in Zagreb, Banja Luka, then back to Zagreb, and then finally in Varazdin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you now or have you ever been a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: No. I have never been a member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Starting with 1991, were you in Banja Luka through the whole year of 1991, or not?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were conditions like in Banja Luka during the year 1991?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: There was quite a bit of tension between the different sides. People simply didn't know what would happen because the war had already begun in Croatia and Slovenia prior to that. There was tension. I'm not sure how I should explain that. There was a feeling among the people. Tensions were high, and the living standards were low. There was a lot of tension, and many people were unemployed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll go into that in a little while. I want to ask you, were you mobilised during that period at all?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: In 1991, month of September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you mobilised to? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: I was transferred from the Kozara barracks to the Stari Gradiska barracks, which is in present-day Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of a unit were you assigned to there?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: The JNA. It was still everyone's army back then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But were you in any particular kind of a company or kind of a unit, or was it just an infantry company or what?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: It was some sort of a signals unit with the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any non-Serbs serving in that unit?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. My superior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- your commander, you mean?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: The commander, yes. The company commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: He is a Croat. His name is Josip, and I cannot remember his last name now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he continue to serve in that capacity all the time that you were with that unit?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other persons in the unit of non-Serb ethnicity other than your commander?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time, then, when you left the army and took a different position?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: No, I asked to be transferred to the police.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness's other microphone, please, kindly be turned on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was it you asked to be transferred to the police?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: In 1992, I just got married, and it was on account of that that I requested a transfer to the public security station in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that transfer granted?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The transcript reflects that you said yes. So then you went from Stara Gradiska back to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was -- what month of 1992 did you return to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what month? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: April, May, June, thereabouts. I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of an impact was the war situation having on the economy in Banja Luka? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: A disastrous one. The economy had ceased to operate. At that time, you could no longer move about, export or import the basic supplies or raw materials. So the economy was in shambles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know people who lost their jobs during 1992?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Especially in production companies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why were people losing their jobs? Did it have to do with the economy?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Mostly, yes, with the economy. 99 per cent, I'd say at the time due to the state of the economy because the biggest, most important companies in Banja Luka had ceased to operate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did -- the issue of whether or not you would lose a job, did that depend on your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Not to the extent that I was aware, or not at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. Could the ELMO be moved, please. I'm just having some difficulty seeing the witness testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, please. Thank you. Wait because you're pulling the wires. See if you can turn it. Is that better, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any members of your family dismissed from employment?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, my sister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it your sister is a Serb?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. The company had ceased to operate. There was nothing to do. It was the Vita Minka [phoen] factory in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about from your wife's family? Any members of your wife's family dismissed from their jobs?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: No, no close relation. At least not the ones I knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've heard a lot in this case about non-Serbs leaving Banja Luka during this time. Do you know why non-Serbs were leaving Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Well, the economic situation was like that. It was as simple as that. People were tense. The war had already begun. People were walking about town armed. This was a situation that proved very difficult to control. And there wasn't much safety. But again, the greatest factor was the economic situation. There were no salaries in Banja Luka to be paid. The inflation rate was so high that you couldn't even afford to buy a box of matches for your salary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were Serbs leaving also?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Quite a number of younger ones, but mostly they were leaving for Serbia since it was difficult to get the appropriate documents to go anywhere else. And then it was through the embassies that the Serbs tried to go to third countries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about in your wife's family? Did members of your wife's family leave the Banja Luka area?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which members of her family left?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Her mother and her father had exchanged their flat for someone else's that was in Zagreb. That was in July or August. They moved there. My mother-in-law worked for Jelsingrad to the very last day. She stopped working maybe seven days before she moved. And my wife's father had already retired. There was an uncle who had obtained documents to travel to America, and they had exchanged their house in exchange for one in Daruvar as well as her grandparents. And there was an aunt who had exchanged her flat for one in Rijeka in Croatia. That was back in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that your wife's mother continued working up until just a few days before they left. I take it she was --

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Croat?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told the Chamber that they -- your wife's family, her mother and father, exchanged their property with someone in Zagreb. Did that exchange --

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you know, that exchange worked out okay?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were happy with it?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Mostly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time they left Banja Luka, did the authorities confiscate any property from them, any money, any valuables, anything like that? Was any of their property confiscated?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they leave because someone forced them to leave, or did they leave because they wanted to leave?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: I can only talk about my family. I'm telling you about my mother-in-law. She set up a company in Croatia, and she just wanted to go there. She was trying to get the appropriate documents to set up a company in Zagreb, and she still owns the company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All these questions I'm asking you about your mother-in-law and father-in-law, did they leave because they had heard politicians make speeches of any kind? Did that frighten them and cause them to leave?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I now want to talk to you, Mr. Golic, about your work on the police force. You say you came to Banja Luka in March, April, May, something like that, of 1992, when you were transferred to the police?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you done police work before that time?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you undergo any kind of training?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. You needed to have completed your secondary education, and then there was a brief course where you were trained in the basics of your service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then did you begin to work as a police officer or what kind of work were you assigned to do?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: I was immediately transferred to the security platoon. We provided security for persons and buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, during that period of 1992, were the police making any distinction in their investigations between whether the victim of a crime was a Serb or a non-Serb?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to talk to you now about Radoslav Brdjanin. You know Mr. Brdjanin, don't you?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you first meet Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: In October or November 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the occasion for your meeting him? How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: I had been assigned to guard his house, and then his wife invited us in, and Radoslav Brdjanin arrived, so that's when I met him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you assigned to guard his house? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: His car had been broken into two or three times, and his windscreen had been stolen. A gas bottle from the balcony or something. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was it that made the decision that you should be assigned there as security?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: The chief of the Security Services Centre, they made assessments of which buildings had to be secured, and then you would receive a document or an order, if you like, detailing your task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, what was Mr. Brdjanin's position at the time you were assigned to security at his house?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: The deputy of the autonomous region. Truth to tell, I wasn't even aware of that back then. Or perhaps he was a minister. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. When you first met Mr. Brdjanin and told him why you were there, to guard his house, to be security, did he accept that? Was that something that he wanted and had asked for? Or do you know?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: He said he didn't need security to begin with. We weren't sent to guard him personally, but rather the building itself, the house. As far as I know, that was the reason that we had been sent there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that his wife had invited you inside. Was that --

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that what was supposed to happen, or not?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: It was completely up to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's normal in that part of the world, Mr. Ackerman. I can confirm that to you. In fact, you would be considered snobbish and not respectful if you don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to tell you that even in England it happens. Not just that part of the world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would imagine so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you working -- was that a -- was that a 24-hour a day proposition, guarding that house, or was it just a nighttime guarding, or how did -- how was that organised?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: From 22 minutes past midnight to 6.00 in the morning. It was nighttime duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there another officer assigned as well as you? Did you take turns, or how did that work?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, two a shift, just to keep it more interesting because it can get a bit boring during the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. In connection with this after you had met Mr. Brdjanin, did you get to know him reasonably well?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get to know his family?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Judges about his family. Does he have children?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, he has two daughters, a wife, and a grandchild.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the names of his daughters?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Jelena and Milka. His wife's name is Mira.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how old are his daughters?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Jelena, I believe, is 19, and little Milka, 25. I can't be sure, however.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one of them apparently has a child that is Mr. Brdjanin's grandson?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how old he is?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Three months, four months maybe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about education? What kind of work? What kind of work -- what kind of education have the girls got?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Jelena was a secondary school student, but now she is studying in Belgrade. And Milka had completed an actors' academy, an acting academy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is she working as an actress?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, she is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this process of getting to know Mr. Brdjanin's family, did you learn about any of his close relatives, brothers, sisters, brother-in-laws, sister-in-laws, that sort of thing? Did you ever get to know any of them, meet any of them, anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I had. On a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many brothers does Mr. Brdjanin to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are both of them married?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber about their wives?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Well, his elderly brother Ilija, his wife is Croatian. And they live in Banja Luka, and they lived there throughout the war. His younger brother, Nebojsa, he was a JNA officer in Ljubljana. He was transferred to Belgrade, and his wife is also a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Nebojsa during the war in Croatia? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: I know that he was attached to the army. He was an active officer in the army. When the army was withdrawing from Slovenia and Zagreb, he then left to Belgrade. Then he left the army and he got a job in a firm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Have you been at Mr. Brdjanin's home for social occasions of any kind, parties, things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of occasions would these be?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: There were celebrations, the Slava birthday, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you invited there along with your wife to parties like that?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other people in attendance besides your wife that were non-Serb at these parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It might be helpful to get a time frame that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay, all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend a Slava at Mr. Brdjanin's house in 1992, 1993, 1994, any of those years?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us as you sit here today how many? Which of those years you attended Slavas or all of them?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: I believe 1993 and 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than your wife, were there other persons in attendance at these Slavas who were non-Serb?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, the wives of his brothers, and he had also friends who had mixed marriages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any of those people?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Aco, and Srebrenka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Aco?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And married to?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about his neighbours? Did he have any neighbours that were non-Serb that were invited to those parties?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. He had a neighbour who was a Muslim named Stacic [as interpreted]. I can't remember his name. He was a prominent person. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you observe the relationship between Mr. Brdjanin and this Muslim neighbour? Did they seem to get along well?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they socialise together other than at these Slavas?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, I know that his wife would come and drink coffee with the neighbour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Brdjanin has any relatives who are married to Muslims?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were working there at the house, was Mr. Brdjanin making trips anywhere?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, he only travelled to Pale. It is where the assembly meetings were held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you ever make that trip to Pale with him?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, on two or three occasions in order to see Pale. I've never been there before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you just went to see Pale and to just basically keep him company on the trip?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of those trips and other times, too, did you have occasion to have conversations with Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to determine results of those conversations what kind of an attitude he had toward non-Serb peoples?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Well, he acted normally. He was never underestimating the others when speaking in this context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear him, in any of your conversations with him, make any kind of a derogatory remark about Serb people -- about non-Serb people? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The security job that you had at Mr. Brdjanin's house, you've already told us, was just a nighttime job. Were there other politicians in Banja Luka who had security assigned to them?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that just night, or were there some who had security 24 hours?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were others who had it 24 hours a day. They had security and a driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a driver, did you say?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the people who you know had 24-hour security and had a driver.

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: The president of the municipality; the chief of the public security centre; and the president of SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the names of those people?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: No. Zupljanin, Stojan, the chief of the centre of social security. Then the chief of the municipality, Predrag Radic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how about the SDS person?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: And the president of SDS was Vukic. I can't remember his first name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Brdjanin have a driver assigned to him?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was no official car and no official driver --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ackerman, because the interpreters did not get his reply. I heard him say "no," if I heard him well. But please, could you answer the question that was put to you by Mr. Ackerman again. Did Mr. Brdjanin have a driver assigned to him? What did you answer? What was your reply to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'll object to the question which we can see on the transcript which was starting. It's being phrased in a leading manner. Unless I'm wrong, he hasn't yet spoken about whether there was an official car. He should just be asked whether there was one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Brdjanin assigned any kind of an official car at any time that you know about?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: An official car from the SUP, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he would go to assembly meetings in Pale, how would he get there? What car would he take?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: He drove his Toyota or took the car of the Ministry of Construction. They had only one car. But usually he drove his own Toyota.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you just your sense of Mr. Brdjanin's power in the Krajina or in Republika Srpska. Do you think he was a very powerful man?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: No. No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever ask him for any kind of help?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Explain to the Chamber what kind of help you asked him for and what happened.

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: When my father in 1995 -- he was operated in 1993 and he was retired at the time, and in 1995 he was mobilised. We attempted, I myself and Radoslav, through the chief of the military department not to mobilise him because he was already 57, 58 years old at the time. But we didn't succeed, and he was sent to Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if any members of Mr. Brdjanin's family were mobilised in the army?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You already talked about his brother Nebojsa who was in the JNA. Anybody else?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. His sister's both sons, one of them was even killed. Then Ilija's daughter as a physician, she was mobilised, and she worked for two or three years near Brcko in a hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if the relatives of prominent people during this time served in the army on the front, or did the prominent people do things to keep their relatives out of those kind of harmful situations? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Well, the majority of them were studying in Serbia, from 18 to 40 years of age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall a time in 1993 when the army came to Mr. Brdjanin's house?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: In front of the house, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber about that and explain as much as you know what that was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I guess I'd ask the time in 1993 and what the relevance is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can tell you, September, Mr. Nicholls. Was it September, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have had evidence on this. We've heard evidence on this, and even -- either you or the Defence, that I don't remember, tendered documents referring during Mr. Radic's testimony. And his involvement as such in trying to neutralise what was supposed to have taken place or what was supposed to take place. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why they came to Mr. Brdjanin's house?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Not exactly. They wanted to search the house and take them to the station to interrogate them. That was the explanation they gave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "take them to the station to interrogate them," who would that have been?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Probably it meant his wife and him because the children were minors. I think that at the time, Brdjanin was at Pale, and Mira was the only one at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they successful in arresting her and taking her in for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: No. We didn't allow them to enter even the entrance. We wanted to be shown a warrant for that, and they didn't have it. And that was in the morning, 5.00 a.m., 5.30 a.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so you basically confronted them, and they backed down after you had confronted them and demanded a warrant?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. They said that they would go to the chief and find the paper and bring the paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they ever come back, then?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: No. Maybe they did, but you see, as it was dawn, we took Mira and the children to their friends outside Banja Luka, to Stojan's, for a few days until the situation calmed down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you took steps to protect them from this army group, I take it, then? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's all questions I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And with regard to this, this is not exactly the details that we've heard -- were not in the article that I was referring to that was tendered during the testimony of Mr. Radic. There were other details, but anyway... You've finished, Mr. Ackerman, I take it. Can you take up the cross-examination right away?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's start with the cross-examination. Cross-examined by Mr. Nicholls:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You live in Banja Luka now?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you born in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than your military service, you lived your whole life in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's where your family is from as well, I take it. Your parents are still there?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me where in Banja Luka you grew up, what neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Starcevica Ada. I have an apartment in Ada, and in Starcevica, a house. So I lived in both of these two neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is Ada predominantly or was it in the early 1990s predominantly a Serb neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Half/half. In Ada, you had a majority of Romas living there, but on the other side of the hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, your present employment, you said you own some kind of a shop. Is that right? What kind of a shop is it that you own in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Flowers, a flower shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I didn't catch it exactly. You also work for an insurance company or something of that nature?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's your job there? Does that have anything to do with security work still?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you do there at the insurance company?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Insurance of property, corporate insurance. You see, we work on evaluating the worth of the firm, and on the basis of that estimate, then we determine what the insurance would be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Could you very briefly just run down for me the employment -- the different kinds of work you've done since, say, the end of 1992. Let me do it this way: When did you leave the police? When did you stop being a policeman?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, since I stopped being a policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, when did you stop being a policeman? What month and year, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: In 1995, when the Dayton Accords were signed. As I didn't want to become an active member of the police, the reserve forces were then fired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After 1992, between that and when you stopped being a reserve member of the police, do you have any other kind of jobs, occupations, businesses, any other activities like that?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: No. From 1992 till 1995, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you this: Your name is relatively rare, wouldn't you say? It's not a common name, Naum Golic.

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of the special unit, the Banja Luka CSB special unit, special detachment?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to show you this document. This is a new one we've found, and we can give out our exhibit list actually. This is ERN 00574836. Sir, this isn't any kind of trick question or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Before you ask any questions, could I see the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While Mr. Ackerman's reading that, I'll just say this is a CSB Banja Luka note from the 14th of June 1993 requesting information on certain police members. If you just read that to yourself, sir, tell me when you've read it.

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Is that, if you know, you being referred to in this document, the Naum Golic who it states was wounded?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I was not in the special brigade of police. I was in the reserve forces. And for 15 days I was in the areas where the fighting was going on, and then a month on the territory of CSB Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of your unit? What was his name?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: I believe at the time when I was in Obadovac that his name was Stojan Davidovic. But I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you were never under the command of Ljuban Ecim?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Heavens forbid it. No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say "heavens forbid" as if that would be a terrible thing?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Well, that unit was constantly in the combat operation zones, and I was once in Obadovac and once near Olovo, and that was all during these three or four years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And we can move on, but that unit, the special unit, wasn't just involved in combat operations; they were involved in a lot of criminal activity as well, weren't they? You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just - best you can - give me the dates of when you were actually in combat and where you were. You've already said Obadovac.

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot give you the date. Obadovac, near Brcko, and Srednje, near Olovo. Maybe I could give you the year, but the dates, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay. Was that the only time you were involved in combat activity after you'd returned to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, this document, will it be an exhibit; and if so, what will its number be?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't think it's a particularly crucial document, but I'll admit it as P2717.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, shortly after you returned to Banja Luka, maybe a couple months after you returned, you started working a security detail for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was Mr. Brdjanin's house then? When you first went to that house, where in Banja Luka was he living?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: It was an apartment in the local commune Starcevica, on the opposite side of Starcevica where I live.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say it was an apartment, what kind of a place was it? Can you describe it, a little bit, the size of it, the grounds? Was it a nice neighbourhood? Just describe where he lived.

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: It was a three-room apartment. These are smaller buildings with four apartments. And when the neighbours -- we would greet all the neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ackerman asked you about what Banja Luka was like in 1992 after you came home from Croatia. And you talked about the economic conditions. And you started to talk about how there were armed groups. But the fact is that Banja Luka in 1992, in the summer, was a very dangerous place. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were bombs going off at businesses almost every night?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: People were walking about armed, those who had arrived from the front were walking around with rifles. And who could have told them, "leave those rifles at home"? You know, as soon as they saw them walking by, everyone just ducked. There were people who were drunk and who were walking around armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were bombs going off at businesses almost every night. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Not quite every night, but...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Three times a week then? Three or four?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts. Well, people didn't move about very much. I wasn't aware exactly what was happening in Budzak. There was a shortage of fuel, and people moved about as little as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you. You're doing fine. I just want to explain when I ask a question, if possible, just answer the question I asked you. All I was asking you about was the frequency of businesses being bombed, not about whether people were moving about. In addition, there were shootings at night, people shooting in the air, shooting recklessly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He hasn't answered your first question as yet, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I thought he had when he said "yes, thereabouts," to explosions three or four times a week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see it, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there were also shootings at night which scared people. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Predominantly, the population which bore the brunt of these attacks and intimidation was the Muslim population, the Bosniak population. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I object to that. He has not testified there were any attacks and intimidation. He's testified there were gunshots and explosions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Rephrase your question, Mr. Nicholls. It's easier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people who were subject to having their businesses bombed, the people were predominantly Bosniaks. Correct? You know that? You were a policeman then.

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: There were Serb facilities, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't say that no Serb business ever burned down in 1992. The population which suffered the most of these bombings of businesses, businesses being burned down was Bosniak. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the same thing, the shooting was designed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters didn't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you say something? Because the interpreters didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only Bosniaks. The gentleman from the Prosecution said Muslims, but there were Croats, too. More of the businesses were owned by Croats in point of fact, where I come from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we can agree, then, that it was mostly non-Serb businesses which were burned down or bombed during the summer of 1992. Right?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You answered the question, and you said yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, because, again, try to speak into the microphones, please, because sometimes the interpreters cannot hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, for some reason his left microphone has now been turned off. I don't know why both microphones aren't on. They usually are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I noticed that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, my attention is being drawn -- okay. Perhaps, you could also ask him, Mr. Nicholls, while we are at this whether there was a time when the predominance of these bombings or whatever was directed at Croat businesses and whether that remained always the same, or whether there was a shift later on at any given time. In other words, whether Muslim business became the predominant target.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But if I can, first the -- although he answered yes to the last question, it's still not on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let me read you this question again. You answered, but it wasn't recorded.

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said: "I think we can agree then that that it was mostly non-Serb businesses which were burned down or bombed during the summer of 1992. Correct?" Can you please answer that question again.

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard His Honour's query. Was there a time when this campaign was directed more at Bosniak or Croat businesses and did that shift over time?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the word "campaign." There's no evidence that this was a campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour There's a lot of evidence this is a campaign, this is my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No arguments in front of the witness, please. Forget the word "campaign." And could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe there was no difference whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I take it you're telling us that throughout 1992, it was always the majority -- the majority of businesses that were targeted was, throughout 1992, always predominantly Croat rather than Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what I want to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying both equally, Croat and Muslim. Both equally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay, yes, Mr. Nicholls, I won't pursue this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, obviously if somebody's business is blown up, burned down, that also affects their employment and would make them want to leave. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Their employment, yes. Because then they would sublet the business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. It wouldn't maybe possibly make somebody want to leave if their business was blown up one night? That might not frighten them a little bit?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So people weren't leaving Banja Luka, Bosniaks and Croats, just because of the economy. Correct? They were also leaving because they were frightened by these bombings, by these armed groups, by these shootings?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said before, it was because of the economy and also because of the tension and the shooting. I believe I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, one thing I think you talked to the Defence about when you met with them was the SOS in Banja Luka. Correct? Serbian Defence Forces?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you met with Defence counsel, I don't know who you met with, or their investigator, did you discuss the topic of the activities of the SOS in Banja Luka in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: We called it SOS. Perhaps that's the reason I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That's what I was trying to call it. Did you -- answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Briefly, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you in Banja Luka when the SOS blockaded the city during the first week of April?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we know that you arrived in Banja Luka sometime in March?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: March or April, thereabouts. Difficult to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if it was April, it was April 1st, wasn't it? Because the blockade was on the 3rd, and you said you were there.

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'm not sure about the dates. It's a bit difficult to remember the dates. My wife went to university at that time, so that's why I remember the rough date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I don't expect you to remember every date from over ten years ago, don't worry about that. I just wanted to confirm that you were present in Banja Luka when the SOS blockaded the town.

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these men were flat out criminals. Correct? No other way to describe them.

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: No other way. 99 per cent of those, we can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This doesn't quite make sense, at least the way it shows on the monitor, or on the transcript. The question that Mr. Nicholls put to you, sir, is: "Now these men were flat out criminals. Correct? No other way to describe them." And what we have is: "No other way. 99 per cent of those, we can't." Could you finish that sentence or could you answer the question again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most of those were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you know that your -- that Radoslav Brdjanin was a big supporter of the SOS, don't you? Speak up, please.

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That topic never came up when you were sitting around the house or driving to Pale, the SOS?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me quickly show you P154. I have it here highlighted, if that helps. Sir, what I'm going to show you is a Glas article from 21st of April 1992. It's entitled "dismissals according to the wishes of the people." And it's an interview with Radoslav Brdjanin. If you see at the present heading, right where the article begins, it states. The basic -- well, it goes on, but it states: "This is the basic reason for the conversation with Radoslav Brdjanin, the vice president of the Assembly of the -- of the AR Bosnian Krajina and a member of the crisis staff, it says, of the municipality of Banja Luka, charged with putting through the demands already accepted of the Serbian Defence Forces about personnel changes in some of the Banja Luka public and joint stock corporations and institutions." Now, on page 3 of the English which, sir, for you is the highlighted portion which begins at the bottom of the page and continues to the top at the end of the article, there is this question from Glas: "The period for the implementation of the demands of the SOS was 15 April. It is clear that they have not been completely realised. Will this happen, and if so when?" And this is what Mr. Brdjanin answered: "We primarily want to carry out our task in a peaceful and civilised manner. We are trying to get people in certain responsible functions in individual firms to understand that they have to pull out. If they really intend to be stubborn and consistent in keeping their cushy positions, the implementation of this demand will be taken over by the Serbian Defence Forces. I repent that we do not want this to be settled in this way, but if individual people in the Banja Luka companies who have been asked to withdraw do not do so in a period of three days, then members of the SOS will come on to the scene." Glas: "All this is happening at a time when there are certain political ferments in the political ruling circles of Banja Luka and Krajina. Will it be a reason for new misunderstandings?" Brdjanin: "I stress once again that the requests of the SOS for personnel changes will get full support both from the crisis staff of Banja Luka and from the AR Bosanska Krajina." That's what it says, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now there, Mr. Brdjanin states -- well, now you know, don't you, that he supported the SOS? It states here that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman, sorry. Okay. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He states that the demands of the SOS are going to get full support, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's where I'll object. Mr. Nicholls is trying to apparently make the point that Brdjanin supported SOS, and the document says the crisis staff and the AR Bosanska Krajina supported that particular demand. So I think it's -- I think it's not fair to suggest that this shows that Brdjanin was a big supporter of SOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think it's perfectly fair --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- from this article to put this question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I allow the question because Brdjanin here is speaking for the crisis staff of Banja Luka and for the Autonomous Region of Krajina as if he had authority to speak authoritatively on their position. Yes, so go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had no inkling at the time or later that Mr. Brdjanin supported the SOS. This is all brand-new lightning bolt out of the blue to you, is it?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we've already agreed that the SOS were criminals; 99 per cent, you said. Mr. Brdjanin here says that he primarily wanted to carry out his task in a peaceful and civilised manner, apparently not limiting himself to those methods, and states that the SOS will reappear in three days. Now, knowing what you've said about the SOS in Banja Luka, a previous blockade earlier this month, wouldn't that be taken as a threat by the people reading this newspaper?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, this is certainly no proof that he was supporting what it said in the newspapers. You know, there were all sorts of things being stated in the newspapers where I come from. We have all sorts of newspapers that you'd be hard-put to define as serious papers. Therefore, I would take none of these things at face value.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Try to answer the question. For a person in Banja Luka who had experienced the SOS blockade earlier that month, for a Bosniak or for a Croat or actually for anybody, isn't this a threat? If they read in the paper here Mr. Brdjanin stating that unless the demands are fulfilled in three days, the SOS will be back, that's a threat, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you could interpret it that way. I don't know really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And Glas at the time, that was the paper in Banja Luka, wasn't it? That was the major paper.

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: No one read papers back then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No one read papers. No one read a paper? No one? That's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Very, very few people. Nothing was open at the time. Well, let me tell you, it was difficult to move about. Who in their right state of mind would go to a kiosk to get the papers?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me go back a little bit to when you first met Mr. Brdjanin. When did you first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was a lot that the witness said that never made it to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's very bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 35, line 17. He's saying we have all sorts of newspapers. "You'd be hard-put to define as serious papers. Take none of this as face value." And he said also, "I see now who wrote this article. He's not a serious person at all, and his newspaper, too."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've heard --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: None of that got translated and put in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you followed what Mr. Ackerman has just remarked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you say those words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is troublesome. It calls for an explanation. Are the interpreters finding it difficult to follow the witness? Because he doesn't give me the impression that he is talking too fast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You'd agree with me that the -- in 1992, after April, Glas was essentially the paper of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can I have -- can I have a look at the document we've just seen, please, the newspaper. Well, I need the English version obviously because I don't read --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The English translation does not actually have the name of the journalist on it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You read me well, Mr. Nicholls. That's what I wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who's the author of this piece, sir? Who is the one you say --

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Zeljko Kopanj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Nicholls, because I want to clear this up. Perhaps Mr. -- usher, this is all that the witness had? Or did he have a second page? Can he show us where the name of the -- here it is, here. Yes, what do you know about this Andjelko Kopanj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what can I tell you? I have had plenty of opportunity to reassure myself when I read the papers that what he wrote was simply not true. Now there's an independent paper where he takes part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you passed the remark on him, according to Mr. Ackerman, and you have confirmed, namely, that this person...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm told, Your Honour, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's not a serious person at all. That's what Mr. Ackerman pointed out to us, and you confirmed that you had stated that he is not a serious person at all. I don't mean Mr. Ackerman, I mean Mr. Kopanj. Why isn't he a serious person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant about writing his articles. Sometimes he twists things around to mean quite the opposite, so that's what I had in mind when I said that. And he continues to do so even today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Anyway, he's -- usher, you can have this back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had misread the note regarding his prior answer. He said --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this constant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has answered the question already. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He said that he's not a serious person at all. And then the last part that I couldn't read properly I'm now told that he referred to his current newspaper, that he's also not serious in his current newspaper where he's working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just, Your Honour, before the break, I'd prefer that we just ask the question again. If he says the answer is incomplete --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Put the question again, Mr. Nicholls. You're free to put the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think this is cleared up at this point. But in principle, we don't know that the interpretation -- I'm not suggesting anything deliberate, but there may be a mistake on that side. The interpreters may have gotten it correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was he already known at the time, in 1992, when this article or this interview appeared in Glas? Was he already known as a nonserious journalist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm telling you is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... Did he have that reputation already at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't answer this question. I simply don't know, the time you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, at the time, the date of the article. We're talking of April of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a lot younger, too young perhaps to pass judgement on that back at the time. I was not involved in that. And I was not involved in politics. I think I was 23 back then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you have no idea about what his reputation was back then. Back then you've already stated you didn't read the newspapers. Right?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you can have no judgement on how the credibility of this article would have been viewed by the population in Banja Luka in 1992? You can't tell us anything about that, can you?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: I can't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And do you remember any conversation that you might have had with Mr. Brdjanin on this particular article or on this particular report of his interview? Never mentioned that to you? He never complained that he was misinterpreted or misquoted by this guy, by this journalist in Glas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember right now precisely which journalists he talked about. But he often complained to me about misinterpreted. When I say "often," I mean twice, perhaps three times. He told me things, and that was my conclusion. I'm not sure I can guarantee specifically about this article, but it did happen quite a number of times that he was misquoted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Shall we break now. We'll break for 25 minutes. How much longer do you think you need, Mr. Nicholls, so that we can programme our day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's getting a little longer than I thought to be honest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I realise that. But it can become shorter now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll definitely finish today. I can say that for sure. My outline is very short. Probably in the next session, but maybe just a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just want the record to show that my direct examination was 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like the record to show that I think that is entirely irrelevant to how long my cross is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Anything else, Mr. Ackerman? Mr. Nicholls? You've said enough, you think. All right. So let's have a break of 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you stated that you don't remember -- you're not sure whether Mr. Kopanj is one of the journalists that Mr. Brdjanin complained about to you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're talking now about -- we're talking about the complaints made by Mr. Brdjanin from the time you met him, first started providing security for him, up to, I don't know, for the next several years. Right?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in all that time, you heard Mr. Brdjanin complain about being misquoted two or three times?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you say this journalist was not serious.

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Now, yes. At least, to my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He published articles which exposed crimes, serious crimes, committed by Serb forces, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Time frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman is right, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, at any time did he publish articles, to your knowledge, which exposed committed by Serb forces from 1992 on?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Of all three peoples, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he published articles about, amongst other things, the massacre at Vlasic mountain, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: His paper published that, but I don't think he was the author of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His paper published that article, and that article was true, wasn't it? You don't dispute that, do you?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, the article was true, just to be clear for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to this journalist, Mr. Kopanj, in 1999?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: A bomb was placed under his car, but from what I heard, it was in connection with some -- connections with crime and scandal. There was a series of articles being published concerning crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who was it who told you who knew precisely why this bomb was placed under this man's car and blew his legs off?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Well, that was what was being said in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So that was a rumour; that wasn't some high-level contact in the police department --

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: He also stated once in the papers that prior to that, he also was receiving threats from that side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So far, I fail to understand on what basis the witness has characterised this journalist as a "nonserious one".

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think you're right, Your Honour. I haven't -- I wasn't actually pursuing that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But why do you say that this journalist is not serious. You've admitted that that story published about that terrible massacre was a correct one, or published in his paper? What was nonserious? And if you want to, what was nonserious about the interview you read with Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that that paper -- that interview wasn't serious but that that journalist and paper that he writes things which are not serious, and he must then carry out two or three rectifications and apologise to those people. It happened with Telekom, the Telekom. The railroad, that was the latest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can move to something else, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me again when you first met Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: It was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What month? September? I'm sorry. I can't remember exactly what you said.

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Well, it was the end. It was in autumn or beginning of winter. Somewhere in October or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And right from the beginning, from your first contact with his family, they invited you in and treated you warmly?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not only towards me; they also -- that was their attitude towards my colleague with whom I worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of your colleague?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Boris Dimitrasinovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how long -- when was the last time that you in any capacity provided security in any capacity for Mr. Brdjanin? I mean, what was the last time? When was the last time you directly guarded his house, went to Pale with him, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Well, as long as he was the minister in the Government of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that -- and throughout that time, you continued to have these warm relations with his family?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't just provide security; you attended social events, parties?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: After that, I wasn't securing his house any more. But we would visit each other, and we would socialise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And you mentioned that he's got a three-month old I think you said grandson or granddaughter?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, a grandson.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen this baby? Have you seen the grandson?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you see the grandson?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: A month ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you're still connected closely to the Brdjanin family?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. We visit each other for the Slavas. We see each other two, three times a year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. I'm just trying to get that straight. You've had a relationship for over ten years with Mr. Brdjanin's family. Now you originally showed up because the windshield had been broken of his Toyota or something like that. Right?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: When the car was broken into.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah. Maybe I misunderstood you. His car was broken into, something like that. So you were assigned to provide --

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Well, there was this report which came in from the SUP. After that, there was another break-in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask: Do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: NAUM GOLIC
utterances.text: Not very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
